assumptions: assumed: week-2 retention for the referral-campaign cohort is roughly 12 percentage points below other channels' cohorts from the same period, as posed by the interviewer
assumed: the referral campaign offered a first-ride discount to new riders
assumed: surge-pricing frequency was similar across cities for both the referral cohort and the comparison cohort
followUps: How would you separate 'the discount attracted one-time deal-seekers' from 'the first-ride experience itself was worse for this cohort'?
If the referred riders' first rides disproportionately hit surge pricing, how would that change your read of this data?
How would you design a referral incentive that's less likely to attract one-time-only users in the first place?

stages.walkthrough: I'll assume the referral cohort's week-2 retention runs about 12 percentage points below other channels in the same period, that the campaign offered a first-ride discount, and that surge-pricing exposure was similar across cohorts, so a pricing-experience difference isn't my starting suspicion. My plan: cover the product context briefly, then build a metric framework isolating whether this is a discount-driven quality issue or a genuine first-ride experience issue, and close with a goal for the referral program.

Rapido's business depends on riders forming a low-cost, convenient habit for short urban trips, competing against both other ride-hailing options and simply walking or using public transit for very short distances, so a new rider's first couple of rides are disproportionately important for establishing that habit before they default back to an alternative. Referral programs are a common low-cost-per-acquisition growth lever, but they inherently risk attracting people motivated primarily by the one-time discount rather than an ongoing need. The mission this connects to is building an everyday, trusted alternative to short-distance travel, which a discount-driven referral spike can undermine if the resulting riders were never going to become habitual users regardless of the actual ride experience.

The ecosystem players are new riders (value = an affordable, quick first-ride experience worth repeating), referring existing riders (value = a reward for a successful referral), and Rapido (value = a low-cost acquisition channel that still produces habitual riders, not just one-time discount users). To diagnose the gap, I'd first check whether the referral cohort's second-ride rate (did they even take a ride beyond the discounted first one) differs meaningfully from other channels, since if most of the retention gap is explained by riders never returning after the discounted ride specifically, that points to discount-seeking behaviour rather than a bad experience. I'd also check first-ride completion quality for the referral cohort specifically (driver wait time, ride cancellation rate, fare accuracy versus the shown estimate) compared to other channels' first rides, since if the referral cohort's first-ride experience was measurably worse, the gap could instead be a genuine service-quality issue concentrated on new riders in whichever cities or times referral campaigns were heaviest.

Assuming the diagnosis shows the gap is concentrated in riders who never took a second ride at all, rather than a worse first-ride experience, I'd set a goal for the growth team on second-ride conversion within 14 days specifically for referral-acquired riders, not on raw referral volume. I'd target closing a defined share of the gap versus other channels next quarter, defended by testing a smaller first-ride discount paired with a second-ride incentive instead of a single large first-ride-only discount, reasoning that spreading the incentive across the first two rides gives riders a reason to return before the campaign's cost-efficiency advantage over other channels is judged solely on volume. This bridges strategy to execution because the growth team directly controls the referral incentive structure, while an overall cost-per-retained-rider guardrail (not just cost-per-signup) ensures the referral program isn't optimized to look cheap on paper while producing riders who never really stick.

pitfalls: Judging a referral channel purely on cost-per-signup without checking whether its second-ride conversion is meaningfully worse than other channels
Assuming a lower-retention referral cohort means the ride experience was bad, without first checking whether they simply never returned after redeeming the one-time discount

cases.title: Diagnose a flattened repeat-purchase curve for Nykaa's loyalty cohort
cases.prompt: Nykaa's month-2 repeat-purchase rate for a recent new-customer cohort flattened at a lower level than the prior four cohorts. As the retention PM, how would you diagnose the cause and set a goal to recover it?
context: Nykaa is an Indian beauty and personal care e-commerce platform that also operates physical retail stores.
Nykaa sells both third-party brands and its own private-label beauty products.
Nykaa listed on Indian stock exchanges in 2021.
assumptions: assumed: month-2 repeat-purchase rate for this cohort is roughly 7 percentage points below the average of the prior four cohorts, as posed by the interviewer
assumed: the cohort's first-purchase basket composition (mix of categories bought) is similar to prior cohorts
assumed: no sitewide pricing or shipping-fee change occurred during this cohort's first two months
followUps: How would you distinguish an assortment/stock-availability problem from a genuine shift in what this cohort wants to buy?
If the flattening were concentrated only in customers whose first purchase was a specific product category, how would that change your investigation?
How would you set a goal here differently for a merchandising/inventory team versus a lifecycle-marketing team?

stages.walkthrough: I'll assume month-2 repeat-purchase rate for this cohort sits about 7 percentage points below the trailing four-cohort average, that first-purchase basket composition looks similar to prior cohorts, and that no sitewide pricing or shipping change happened during this window, so my starting suspicion is something more specific, like assortment or stock availability for repeat-purchase items. My plan: briefly frame Nykaa's business context, build a metric framework to isolate where in the repeat-purchase journey the flattening lives, and close with a goal split across the teams that could act on it.

Nykaa's business model depends heavily on repeat purchases of consumable beauty products (skincare, makeup that gets used up and repurchased), so a flattened month-2 repeat-purchase curve directly threatens lifetime value, not just an engagement metric. Its private-label and exclusive-brand assortment is a key competitive differentiator against generic e-commerce marketplaces, meaning assortment health (in-stock rates on frequently-repurchased items) matters more for Nykaa's retention than for a platform selling interchangeable commodity goods. The mission this connects to is being the trusted, go-to destination for a customer's ongoing beauty routine, which depends on customers being able to reliably reorder what they already love.

The ecosystem players are customers (value = reliably being able to reorder trusted products), brand partners including Nykaa's own private labels (value = a growing base of repeat buyers), and Nykaa (value = high customer lifetime value driven by repeat, not one-time, purchases). To diagnose the flattening, I'd first check repeat-purchase rate specifically for customers whose first purchase included a product that later went out of stock or was discontinued during their second-month window, since a stock-availability problem on frequently-repurchased items would show up precisely as a lower repeat rate concentrated in exactly that customer subset, with the rest of the cohort behaving normally. I'd also check whether this cohort's first-purchase products skew toward a category with historically lower repurchase cadence (for instance, a one-time gifting item versus a regular skincare consumable), which would look like a retention problem but actually reflect a natural, expected difference in category-level repurchase timing. If the flattening is spread evenly across all product categories and stock-availability is unaffected, that would point toward something broader, like a lifecycle-marketing or reminder-email change that stopped reaching this cohort effectively.

Assuming the diagnosis shows the flattening concentrates on customers whose repurchase-relevant product went out of stock, I'd set a goal jointly owned by merchandising/inventory and lifecycle marketing: an in-stock rate target for the top repeat-purchase-driving SKUs, alongside a month-2 repeat-purchase-rate recovery target for customers affected by that stockout. I'd target recovering the majority of the 7-point gap within a quarter, defended by the size of the affected SKU's contribution to this cohort's first-purchase basket and by the assumption that restocking plus a targeted reminder to affected customers once the item is back can recapture most of the lapsed repeat-purchase intent. This bridges strategy to execution because inventory directly controls the stock-availability lever while lifecycle marketing directly controls re-engaging the affected customers, and an overall repeat-purchase-rate guardrail across all cohorts ensures this fix doesn't just move the problem to a different cohort or category.

pitfalls: Assuming a flattened repeat-purchase curve is a marketing or engagement problem before checking whether a specific frequently-repurchased product simply went out of stock
Comparing repeat-purchase rate across cohorts without accounting for a shift in first-purchase category mix that naturally has a different repurchase cadence

cases.title: Diagnose a week-4 retention gap for Blinkit's newly launched cities
cases.prompt: Week-4 retention for new users acquired in Blinkit's recently launched tier-2 cities is running well below retention for equivalent new-user cohorts in its established metro markets. As the PM for new-market expansion, how would you diagnose this and set a goal?
context: Blinkit (formerly Grofers) is an Indian quick-commerce grocery delivery platform promising delivery within minutes from local dark stores.
Blinkit was acquired by Zomato (now Eternal) in 2022.
Blinkit competes with other quick-commerce players such as Zepto and Swiggy Instamart in Indian cities.
assumptions: assumed: week-4 retention for new-city cohorts runs roughly 15 percentage points below equivalent-tenure cohorts in established metros, as posed by the interviewer
assumed: these new tier-2 cities launched with fewer dark stores per capita than the established metros had at the same point in their own launch history
assumed: delivery promise time (minutes) shown to users is the same nationally regardless of actual local fulfillment capacity
followUps: How would you tell whether this is a delivery-experience problem versus these cities simply having lower category fit for quick-commerce overall?
If dark-store density is the driver, would you recommend slowing new-city launches or accepting lower retention as a temporary cost of expansion?
How would you set a goal here that doesn't unfairly penalize a new-market team for a structural, not execution, gap?

stages.walkthrough: I'll assume week-4 retention for new tier-2 city cohorts runs about 15 percentage points below equivalent-tenure metro cohorts, that these cities launched with lower dark-store density per capita than metros had at a comparable stage, and that the delivery-time promise shown to users doesn't yet adjust for local fulfillment capacity. My plan: frame the business context briefly, build a metric framework that isolates whether this is a delivery-experience gap tied to density, a genuine category-fit gap, or something else, and close with a goal appropriately split between expansion and operations teams.

Blinkit's entire value proposition rests on a specific, fast delivery-time promise, which is only achievable when dark-store density is high enough relative to local demand; expanding into new cities before that density is built is a deliberate growth trade-off, not a mistake, but it does mean new cities structurally start below the experience level that established metros offer. Competitively, all major quick-commerce players race for density and coverage in new cities simultaneously, so a slower, more cautious density build-out risks ceding early-mover advantage to a competitor. The mission this connects to is making minutes-fast delivery a reliable everyday habit, which depends on the delivery promise actually being met, not just advertised, in every city Blinkit operates in.

The ecosystem players are new-city customers (value = the same fast, reliable delivery promise as any metro customer), dark-store operations teams (value = enough local demand to justify the store's cost), and Blinkit (value = sustainable growth into new markets without diluting its core promise). To diagnose the gap, I'd check actual delivered time versus the promised time for orders in these new cities compared to metros, since if new-city orders are taking meaningfully longer than what's shown to the user at checkout, that's a direct, measurable trust-breaking gap rather than a vague 'new market adjustment' story. I'd also segment retention by distance from the nearest dark store within these cities, since if retention is meaningfully better for users living close to a store and meaningfully worse for those farther away, that isolates density (a fixable, ops-side variable) as the driver rather than these cities simply having lower underlying demand for quick-commerce as a category. If retention were uniformly low regardless of proximity to a dark store, that would instead suggest a category-fit issue -- these markets may just have different shopping habits -- which calls for a different response than building more stores.

Assuming the diagnosis confirms retention correlates strongly with proximity to a dark store, I'd set a goal jointly owned by operations and new-market expansion: a dark-store-density target (stores per capita, or percentage of new-city population within a set delivery-time radius) to reach within two quarters, paired with a week-4 retention target for new cohorts once that density threshold is hit in a given city, rather than expecting current cohorts to close the full gap immediately. I'd defend the density target's size by benchmarking against the density level established metros had reached by the point their own retention matched today's metro baseline. This bridges strategy to execution because operations directly controls store rollout pace, while new-market expansion controls launch sequencing and can choose to delay full-scale user acquisition marketing in a city until density catches up, and an actual-versus-promised delivery-time guardrail ensures the promise isn't overstated to new-city users in the meantime.

pitfalls: Treating lower retention in new cities as an onboarding or marketing problem without checking whether the actual delivery promise is being met there
Setting the same retention target for new and established cities without accounting for the structural density gap driving the difference

cases.title: Diagnose a week-4 retention drop explained by referral-incentive composition on Groww
cases.prompt: Week-4 retention for a recent new-investor cohort on Groww came in well below the trailing average, the same month a large one-time referral bonus campaign ran. As the PM for activation, how would you diagnose this and set a goal for the next quarter?
context: Groww is an Indian investment platform offering mutual funds, stocks, and other investment products through a mobile app.
Opening a Groww account requires KYC verification before a user can begin investing.
Groww has grown its user base partly through referral programs and low-cost, no-brokerage positioning.
assumptions: assumed: week-4 retention (defined as any app open with a portfolio view or new investment action) fell roughly 13 percentage points below the trailing six-month average for this cohort, as posed by the interviewer
assumed: the referral campaign offered a fixed cash bonus to both referrer and referee once the referee completed a small minimum first investment
assumed: KYC completion and first-investment completion rates for this cohort were similar to prior cohorts
followUps: How would you prove the drop is about who the campaign attracted rather than a genuine product issue that happened to coincide with it?
Would you recommend Groww run this kind of referral campaign again? What would you change about its design?
How would you set an activation-team goal without unfairly holding them accountable for a growth-team acquisition decision?

stages.walkthrough: I'll assume week-4 retention for this cohort fell about 13 percentage points below the trailing six-month average, that the referral campaign paid both sides a fixed cash bonus once the referee made a small minimum first investment, and that KYC and first-investment completion rates for this cohort looked normal, meaning the funnel up to first investment wasn't the problem. My plan: frame the business and mission context, build a metric framework that tests whether this is a cohort-composition effect from the incentive design versus a genuine activation problem, and close with a goal appropriately scoped to the activation team.

Groww's business model depends on investors continuing to invest over time, since revenue is tied to ongoing transaction and asset-under-management activity, not a one-time account opening, so a cohort that invests once to claim a bonus and then disengages is close to worthless from a lifetime-value standpoint even though it looks identical to a genuine new investor in top-of-funnel metrics. Competitively, referral-driven growth is a common low-CAC lever across Indian fintech, but a bonus structured around a small minimum investment specifically risks attracting people optimizing for the reward rather than genuinely starting an investing habit. The mission this connects to is helping first-time investors build a lasting investing habit, which a reward-chasing cohort can directly undermine if the incentive isn't designed to select for genuine intent.

The ecosystem players are new investors (value = an easy, low-friction way to start investing), referring existing users (value = a cash reward for a successful referral), and Groww (value = a growing base of investors who keep transacting, not one-time bonus claimants). To diagnose the drop, I'd first check the size and nature of this cohort's first investment: if a large share of the campaign's new investors put in exactly the minimum qualifying amount and never added to it, that's a strong signal the incentive selected for bonus-chasers rather than genuine first-time investors, distinct from Groww's typical organic and non-incentivized-referral cohorts. I'd also compare week-4 retention for this cohort's minimum-investment sub-segment against the sub-segment that invested meaningfully more than the minimum, since if the higher-investment sub-segment's retention looks normal while the minimum-investment sub-segment's retention has cratered, that isolates the incentive's design, not a broader product issue, as the driver. If retention were uniformly low regardless of first-investment size, that would instead point toward a genuine activation-experience problem that happened to coincide with the campaign timing, not the campaign itself.

Assuming the diagnosis confirms the drop concentrates in the minimum-investment, bonus-chasing sub-segment, I'd set a goal jointly with the growth team on future referral-campaign design rather than asking activation to fix retention for a cohort that was never going to convert as designed: specifically, redesigning the incentive to require a meaningfully higher minimum investment, or to pay out the bonus in installments tied to continued activity over the first month. For the activation team specifically, I'd set a goal on week-4 retention excluding future bonus-driven minimum-investment cohorts, protecting the metric from being diluted by acquisition-design choices outside activation's control, while defending the incentive-redesign recommendation with the clear gap shown between the minimum-investment and higher-investment sub-segments in this campaign. This bridges strategy to execution because growth directly controls campaign incentive structure going forward, while activation can be fairly held accountable only for the retention of users it actually has a chance to influence.

pitfalls: Holding the activation team accountable for a retention drop that's actually explained by an acquisition-incentive design decision made by a different team
Assuming all referral-driven users behave the same way without splitting by whether they invested exactly the minimum qualifying amount or genuinely more
